doc.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Younger and older generations of musicians supporting each other
summary: He praises Joe Wilder, Britt Woodman, Sweets Edison and Buster Cooper for encouraging young players and criticizes bitterness among those in between.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: communal thing. It wasn’t about I’m soloing and you know, check out what I’m doing. It was more communal. And I think the guys and ladies, the people that played that music, they were more communal in their approach to life and to each other. And our generation today, because most of the musicians grew up listening to bebop, one thing that I think I dislike is it’s hard sometimes, it seems like a lot of the musicians don’t really get or give props to another musician until after they’re dead and gone. Some of us, I’d say a great majority of the musicians, when we see the guys we haven’t seen in a while, they’re very supportive. But then there’s that generation of musicians that really, for one reason or another, they’re not happy with the way their career went. They are not satisfied with the young lions so to speak. They’re not satisfied with the way their career went and then you have young lions coming up and they’re getting recognition and they were not happy for various reasons. So rather than to deal with the majesty and the music, they began to take it personally and then there’s, for lack of a better term I’ll say confusion, in terms of well who’s supporting who. And you know all the musicians, you know jazz is not, we’re not making millions and millions of dollars playing jazz. Maybe a few people are but it’s not like when you go to a rock concert or to a rap concert, so why in the jazz community should we not support one another? And I think that’s one of the great things about these jazz parties. And I haven’t been, I’m kind of a baby to the jazz party because working with Wynton Marsalis, we were on the road almost three hundred days out of the — I wasn’t available to go to a lot of them. But it’s great when you have someone like Joe Wilder, I’ll say this then I’ll be quiet, or Britt Woodman, they were always supportive of the younger cats. And that doesn’t happen — the generation between Joe Wilder, I’ll say a musician between Joe Wilder and mine, they are always supportive. And even in their teaching. They weren’t patronizing. They were always supportive. Always had something good to say. Always gave a word of encouragement. Sweets Edison, he was the same way. And if he didn’t like something, he didn’t like it. But he would never be like you need to do this, or these young guys they’re not playing anything. He never really had the attitude. And there’s a lot of musicians that are kind of like that. And some of them are guys in our generation. I say well what happened to the spirit of, you know, trying to play? Buster Cooper, he’s another. He’s always, just always, says you young guys are doing it, carrying on the tradition. And there’s always, I think we need those guys to egg us on and to be supportive.

I think you’re right and I think that some of that comes — some of the lack of that I believes comes from this term I heard recently and that was jazz in the middle ages, that the people that are in that generation of being around 50 or so forth, some of them feel that the younger guys are getting all the marketing support and the record company support and what about me.

Right. There’s a lot of that. Joe Wilder doesn’t take on that. He doesn’t take on that attitude. Buster Cooper, he didn’t take on that attitude. Britt Woodman, he didn’t take on that attitude. But some of the guys that are under him, it seems like they’re bitter, it’s like hey man, you could not be playing jazz at all. I mean things haven’t always been great. I mean just like in life, there’s ups and there’s downs, but you take the good with the bad and you just try to roll with it. And I think that’s the spirit that those guys have. Because the time that they come up, in terms of social conditions and whatnot, they were not as great as they are now. So and I say if you have guys that grew up in that time period and they live with a certain amount of optimism, I mean how could you go wrong?
